hypotheses.title: runJackpot refund griefing via reverting receiver blocks drawing
hypotheses.description: runJackpot() refunds excess ETH to msg.sender via a low-level call and reverts the entire transaction if the refund fails. Since runJackpot is permissionless, any caller can supply msg.value > fee and use a contract whose receive/fallback reverts, causing the whole drawing to revert. Because the drawing is time-gated and the lock is only set after the refund, an attacker can repeatedly front-run legitimate callers and prevent the jackpot from ever being drawn.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a contract with a reverting receive(). 2) After drawingTime passes, attacker calls runJackpot{value: fee + 1}() from that contract. 3) The refund call to msg.sender reverts, reverting the whole tx. 4) Attacker repeats (or front-runs) every attempt by honest users, keeping the drawing permanently locked out.
hypotheses.impact: Jackpot cannot be settled; ticket purchases are blocked (jackpotLock stays false but drawing never completes), LP withdrawals are stuck pending, and all funds in the contract are frozen indefinitely.
hypotheses.recommendation: Send the refund via a pull pattern (credit to a mapping) or wrap the refund call in try/catch and ignore failures, so a hostile caller cannot block the drawing.

hypotheses.title: Missing nonce/deadline in claimWinnings signature allows replay
hypotheses.description: The EIP-712 hash for `claimWinnings` includes only ticketIds and bridgeDetails, with no nonce, deadline, or per-call uniqueness. Once a ticket owner signs a claim, the same signature remains valid indefinitely and can be replayed by anyone as long as the ticket ownership check still passes. Because `_validateTicketOwnership` only checks `ticketOwner[ticketId] == signer`, the signature can be re-submitted repeatedly until the ticket is transferred or the jackpot claim reverts.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User signs a claimWinnings signature for their tickets. 2) Attacker observes the signature in the mempool. 3) Attacker front-runs and calls `claimWinnings` with the same signature and bridgeDetails pointing to attacker-controlled `to`/`data`. 4) The signature validates, ownership check passes, jackpot pays out, and `_bridgeFunds` sends the USDC to the attacker's bridge destination. 5) The legitimate user's claim later reverts because tickets are burned.
hypotheses.impact: Direct theft of the user's winnings via front-running; the signed bridge destination is attacker-controlled and the funds are irreversibly bridged away.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include a nonce, deadline, and the intended `msg.sender`/recipient in the signed payload, and store consumed nonces to prevent replay.

hypotheses.title: getUserTickets returns array with zero-fill holes for transferred tickets
hypotheses.description: The view iterates over `totalTicketsOwned` and only fills `ticketIds[i]` when `ticketOwner[ticketId] == _user`. After a `claimTickets` transfer, the entry in `ticketOwner` is deleted but `totalTicketsOwned` and `ticketIds[...]` mapping entries are not updated, so slots are left at 0. Any consumer (off-chain or on-chain) reading this array will see `ticketId == 0` entries that are not valid tickets, potentially confusing downstream integrations or causing wasted claim attempts.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an external attacker; however, an attacker who receives tickets via claimTickets can trigger the stale-index state that downstream integrations rely upon (e.g., a batch claim in `claimWinnings` will revert on a zero ticketId since `ticketOwner[0]` will not match). Any integrator that trusts `getUserTickets` will compute an incorrect ticket list.
hypotheses.impact: Off-chain/on-chain indexers and claim batch builders get incorrect data; integrations may build a batch including ticketId 0 and revert, or may miss that the user no longer owns the ticket. Misreporting of ownership.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compact the ticket list on transfer (swap-and-pop like JackpotTicketNFT._beforeTokenTransfer) rather than leaving zero-filled holes, or return a dynamically-sized filtered array without preallocating to `totalTicketsOwned`.

hypotheses.title: claimTickets signature lacks nonce/deadline and is replayable
hypotheses.description: `createClaimTicketEIP712Hash` binds only `_ticketIds` and `_recipient`, with no nonce, deadline, or chain-specific replay protection beyond the EIP-712 domain. A signature authorizing a transfer to a specific recipient can be replayed by anyone at any time, and the same signature can be reused across multiple calls if the ticket ownership state is restored (e.g., via re-purchase or re-mint of the same ticketId, which is deterministic from drawingId/globalTicketsBought/packedTicket).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User signs a `claimTickets` authorization for recipient R. 2) Attacker observes the signature. 3) Attacker calls `claimTickets` with the same signature; the check `ticketOwner[ticketId] == signer` passes and the NFT is transferred to R. 4) If the same ticketId is later re-minted (deterministic ID) and re-owned by the signer, the same signature can be replayed again to move the ticket without fresh consent.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized ticket transfers and potential loss of ticket ownership; replayable authorization persists indefinitely.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a nonce and deadline to the signed struct, and mark nonces as used; also bind the signature to `msg.sender` if the caller is meant to be the executor.

hypotheses.title: claimTickets signature reusable by front-runner because caller is not bound
hypotheses.description: The EIP-712 hash created by `createClaimTicketEIP712Hash(_ticketIds, _recipient)` binds only the ticket IDs and the recipient; it does not include `msg.sender` or a nonce/deadline. Any external party who observes the signature in the mempool can submit the identical call before the intended caller. Because the recipient is fixed by the signature the attacker cannot redirect the NFTs to themselves, but the attack still causes the honest user's transaction to revert (tickets already transferred, `ticketOwner` deleted) leading to gas loss and race-condition griefing. Signatures never expire since there is no deadline.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Honest ticket owner signs `(ticketIds, recipient)` and submits `claimTickets`. 2) Attacker observes the pending transaction, extracts `_ticketIds`, `_recipient`, `_signature`. 3) Attacker front-runs the transaction, executing the exact same call — the NFTs go to the intended recipient (bounded by signature) but the honest user's subsequent tx reverts with `NotTicketOwner`. 4) Victim loses gas and the transaction fails.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing and wasted gas for users; no fund theft because the signature pins the recipient, but the signature's lack of expiry and lack of caller-binding makes it reusable by anyone who obtains it, creating a denial-of-service vector for every claimTickets call and a persistent risk if the signature leaks.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include `msg.sender` (or an explicit executor field) plus a nonce/deadline in the EIP-712 payload, and enforce it during recovery.

hypotheses.title: claimTickets lacks nonReentrant and updates ownership before NFT transfer
hypotheses.description: `claimTickets` is the only external state-changing function in `JackpotBridgeManager` that is NOT protected by `nonReentrant`. It calls `_updateTicketOwnership`, which deletes `ticketOwner[ticketId]` and then performs `safeTransferFrom` (an ERC-721 callback to the recipient). Because the ownership mapping is cleared before the external call and there is no reentrancy guard, a malicious recipient contract can re-enter `claimTickets` (or `claimWinnings`) during the `onERC721Received` callback.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a valid EIP-712 signature for `claimTickets([id], attackerContract)`. 2) Attacker calls `claimTickets`; inside `_updateTicketOwnership`, `ticketOwner[id]` is deleted, then `safeTransferFrom` invokes `onERC721Received` on the attacker contract. 3) In the callback, the attacker re-enters `claimTickets` with the same `id` and a fresh recipient. Since `ticketOwner[id]` was already deleted, `_validateTicketOwnership` reverts — but the attacker can instead re-enter `claimWinnings` for the same ticket if it has winnings, or re-enter with a different ticket whose ownership was already cleared in the same loop. 4) More critically, the attacker can re-enter `claimWinnings` for the same ticket id before the NFT is actually transferred, since `ticketOwner` is already deleted and `jackpot.claimWinnings` checks `ownerOf` on the NFT (still the bridge manager) — allowing double-claim of winnings.
hypotheses.impact: Double-claiming of jackpot winnings for the same ticket, draining USDC from the bridge manager / jackpot.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `nonReentrant` to `claimTickets` and reorder `_updateTicketOwnership` to transfer the NFT first, then delete `ticketOwner` (or use a checks-effects-interactions pattern with a per-ticket lock).

hypotheses.title: ScaledEntropyProvider callback failure bricks drawing permanently
hypotheses.description: entropyCallback() deletes the pending request before invoking the callback, and reverts with CallbackFailed if the callback reverts. Because the pending request is deleted first, a failed callback cannot be retried — the entropy is consumed and the Jackpot contract's scaledEntropyCallback never runs, leaving the drawing locked (jackpotLock == true) forever. Any condition that makes scaledEntropyCallback revert (e.g., out-of-gas due to entropyGasLimit being too low for the bonusballMax, or a revert in payoutCalculator) permanently bricks the drawing.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or any user) calls runJackpot with a gas limit that is insufficient for the current bonusballMax, or manipulates state so scaledEntropyCallback reverts. 2) entropyCallback deletes the pending request, then the callback reverts. 3) The Jackpot drawing remains locked; no new drawing can start, and LP/ticket funds are frozen.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent lock of the Jackpot contract: current drawing cannot be settled, ticket purchases are blocked, LP withdrawals are stuck, and all funds in the contract are frozen.
hypotheses.recommendation: Do not delete the pending request until the callback succeeds, or allow the owner/anyone to retry the callback with the stored entropy; alternatively, add a recovery path in Jackpot to unlock and re-request entropy.

hypotheses.title: _bridgeFunds uses arbitrary call with no allowlist or value check
hypotheses.description: `_bridgeFunds` performs `_bridgeDetails.to.call(_bridgeDetails.data)` with no allowlist, no selector restriction, and no validation that `to` is a legitimate bridge. The only post-condition is that the USDC balance decreased by exactly `_claimedAmount`. An attacker who controls the signed `_bridgeDetails` (or who can get a user to sign a malicious payload) can make the contract call any address with any calldata, including calling `usdc.transfer` directly to the attacker, or calling `usdc.approve` followed by a transferFrom by the attacker.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker crafts `_bridgeDetails` with `to = USDC` and `data = transfer(attacker, claimedAmount)`. 2) Attacker gets the victim to sign the claim (e.g., via a phishing dApp that displays a different payload). 3) Attacker submits the claim; `_bridgeFunds` calls USDC.transfer to the attacker, balance decreases by claimedAmount, check passes. 4) Funds are stolen.
hypotheses.impact: Direct theft of claimed winnings via arbitrary call to USDC or any other token/contract held by the bridge manager.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `_bridgeDetails.to` to an allowlist of approved bridge contracts and validate the selector/calldata against expected bridge interfaces.

hypotheses.title: Referral win share double-counted when no referral scheme set
hypotheses.description: When a ticket has no referral scheme (`_referralSchemeId == bytes32(0)`), `_payReferrersWinnings` adds `referrerShare` to `drawingState[currentDrawingId].lpEarnings` and returns `referrerShare`. The caller (`claimWinnings`) then subtracts `referrerShare` from `winningAmount` before paying the user, so the user receives `winningAmount - referrerShare`. However, the LP earnings credit is applied to the *current* drawing's `lpEarnings`, which is later used in `scaledEntropyCallback` as `_lpEarnings` for the *current* drawing settlement — but the winning ticket belongs to a *past* drawing whose `prizePool` was already reduced by the payout. The referrer share is thus credited to LPs of the wrong drawing, and the past drawing's LP pool is under-credited while the current drawing's LP pool is over-credited, causing cross-drawing accounting leakage.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker buys tickets in drawing N with no referral scheme. 2) Drawing N settles; attacker's ticket wins. 3) Attacker calls `claimWinnings` during drawing N+1. 4) The referrer share is added to `drawingState[N+1].lpEarnings` instead of being accounted against drawing N's LP pool. 5) Attacker (or any LP) can exploit the inflated `lpEarnings` in drawing N+1 to extract more value via LP shares, or the mis-accounting causes drawing N's LP pool to be short by the referrer share.
hypotheses.impact: Cross-drawing LP accounting leakage; LPs of the winning drawing lose the referrer share while LPs of the current drawing gain it, enabling value extraction by LPs who time deposits/withdrawals around claims.
hypotheses.recommendation: Credit the referrer share to the drawing that the ticket belongs to (pass `drawingId` into `_payReferrersWinnings` and update `drawingState[drawingId].lpEarnings`), or handle it as a direct LP pool adjustment at settlement time.

hypotheses.title: Leftover USDC approval to bridge provider is never revoked
hypotheses.description: `usdc.approve(_bridgeDetails.approveTo, _claimedAmount)` is granted whenever `approveTo != address(0)` but is never reset to 0 after the bridge call. If the bridge route uses only a partial amount (or the bridge rejects/uses less), the residual allowance persists. Also, approvals accumulate across calls to the same approveTo without being cleared; because USDC's `approve` uses allowance-overwrite semantics (in most USDC deployments it sets rather than adds), a subsequent smaller claim can overwrite or leave stale values depending on bridge consumption.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker (a holder of any USDC spender allowance from this contract) reuses the residual allowance to pull USDC that was meant for a different claim, or to pull funds bridged into the contract by a subsequent deposit. Any spender that has ever received an approval and did not consume it fully can drain future balance sitting in the contract (from another user's failed bridge, winnings, etc.).
hypotheses.impact: Loss of funds held in the bridge manager by any address that was previously approved and retained allowance. Inconsistent state (approval left open) beyond the intended bridge.
hypotheses.recommendation: After the bridge call, reset `usdc.approve(_bridgeDetails.approveTo, 0)` (or approve exact and then clear), or use a transient allowance pattern.

hypotheses.title: Bridge manager refunds full ticket price on emergency refund despite referral fees
hypotheses.description: When a ticket was purchased with a referral scheme, the Jackpot contract already paid out `referralFee` to referrers at purchase time (deducted from `lpEarnings`), but `emergencyRefundTickets` refunds the buyer `ticketPrice * (PRECISE_UNIT - referralFee) / PRECISE_UNIT` — i.e., the buyer gets back the post-referral amount while the referrer keeps the fee. However, the refund is paid out of the contract's USDC balance which was funded by the full `ticketPrice`; the referral fee portion was already distributed to referrers and is not clawed back. If many referred tickets are refunded, the contract pays out more than it holds for those tickets, draining LP/prize-pool USDC.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker registers as a referrer with 100% split. 2) Attacker buys tickets via a second address using their own referral scheme, so the full `referralFee` is credited to the attacker's `referralFees` balance. 3) Attacker calls `claimReferralFees()` to withdraw the fee. 4) Owner enables emergency mode (or attacker waits for it). 5) Attacker calls `emergencyRefundTickets` on the same tickets and receives `ticketPrice * (1 - referralFee)` back. Net: attacker recovers nearly the full ticket price while the referral fee was already withdrawn, leaving the contract short by `referralFee` per ticket.
hypotheses.impact: Contract USDC balance drains faster than ticket revenue; LP pool and prize pool become under-collateralized; other LPs/users cannot withdraw or claim.
hypotheses.recommendation: On emergency refund, either claw back the referral fee from `referralFees[referrer]` before refunding, or refund the full `ticketPrice` and deduct the referral fee from the referrer's balance; alternatively, refund only `ticketPrice - referralFee` and require referrers to return fees.

hypotheses.title: getUserTickets returns array with zero-filled gaps after transfers
hypotheses.description: getUserTickets() allocates an array of size totalTicketsOwned and fills index i only when ticketOwner[ticketId] == _user, leaving zero entries for tickets that were transferred away. Since totalTicketsOwned is never decremented on transfer (only ticketOwner is deleted in _updateTicketOwnership), the returned array contains zero-padded holes. Off-chain consumers that iterate the array and pass the IDs to claimWinnings will include ticketId 0, which is not owned by the user, causing _validateTicketOwnership to revert and blocking the claim.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User buys tickets, then calls claimTickets to transfer some away. 2) getUserTickets now returns an array with zero entries. 3) User (or an integrator) passes the returned array to claimWinnings; the zero ticketId fails ownership validation and the whole claim reverts.
hypotheses.impact: Users cannot reliably use the view function to construct claim batches; integrators may build broken transactions, and users may be unable to claim winnings without manual filtering.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compact the returned array (skip non-owned tickets) or decrement totalTicketsOwned on transfer so the array has no holes.

hypotheses.title: _bridgeFunds approves arbitrary spender and calls arbitrary target with no reentrancy guard on approval
hypotheses.description: `_bridgeFunds` performs `usdc.approve(_bridgeDetails.approveTo, _claimedAmount)` and then `_bridgeDetails.to.call(_bridgeDetails.data)` where both `approveTo`, `to`, and `data` are fully attacker-controlled (only constrained by the EIP-712 signature, which the attacker themselves produces for their own tickets). The function is called from `claimWinnings` which is `nonReentrant`, but the approval is left outstanding after the call and the arbitrary `to.call` can invoke any contract, including re-entering `Jackpot` or `JackpotBridgeManager` functions that are not guarded (e.g., `claimTickets`).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker signs a `ClaimWinningsData` with `approveTo = attacker`, `to = attackerContract`, `data = <malicious>`. 2) `claimWinnings` claims winnings, then `_bridgeFunds` approves `attacker` for `claimedAmount` and calls `attackerContract`. 3) `attackerContract` calls `usdc.transferFrom(bridgeManager, attacker, claimedAmount)` using the leftover allowance, then re-enters `claimTickets` (unguarded) to also extract the NFT. 4) The balance check `preUSDCBalance - postUSDCBalance != _claimedAmount` passes because the attacker's `transferFrom` moves exactly `claimedAmount`.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker extracts both the USDC winnings and the underlying ticket NFT, and can leave residual allowance for future drains.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reset allowance to zero after the bridge call, restrict `approveTo`/`to` to a whitelist of trusted bridge contracts, and add `nonReentrant` to `claimTickets`.

hypotheses.title: claimWinnings signature not bound to msg.sender or bridge destination
hypotheses.description: The signed payload includes `_bridgeDetails` (approveTo, to, data) but the contract does not verify that the caller is the signer or that the bridge destination is the intended recipient. Any third party can submit a valid signature and choose the `_bridgeDetails` only if they match the signed hash — but since the signer must sign the exact bridgeDetails, the risk is that the signer may not realize the bridge destination is attacker-controlled. More critically, the signature does not bind `msg.sender`, so a relayer can execute the claim and the funds go to whatever `to` was signed. If the user signs a generic bridgeDetails (e.g., approveTo=0, to=some router), the attacker can substitute a different `data` only if it hashes the same — not feasible — but the lack of `msg.sender` binding still allows front-running with the exact signed payload, which is the replay issue above.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User signs a claim with bridgeDetails pointing to a legitimate bridge. 2) Attacker front-runs with the same signature and bridgeDetails. 3) The claim executes and funds are bridged to the signed destination, but the user's tickets are burned and the user cannot re-claim. 4) If the signed destination is a contract that the attacker can influence (e.g., a router with attacker-controlled calldata), the attacker can redirect funds.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of winnings to front-running; user loses tickets and cannot re-claim.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind `msg.sender` (or an explicit `recipient`) into the signed payload and require the caller to be the signer or an authorized executor.

hypotheses.title: Emergency refund uses current referralFee instead of purchase-time fee
hypotheses.description: `emergencyRefundTickets` computes the refund as `ticketPrice * (PRECISE_UNIT - referralFee) / PRECISE_UNIT` using the *current* `referralFee` state variable, not the referral fee that was in effect when the ticket was purchased. If the owner changes `referralFee` between purchase and emergency refund, users who bought with a referral scheme receive a refund that does not match what they actually paid (the referral fee was already distributed to referrers at purchase time). This can over-refund or under-refund users, and the referrers keep their already-distributed fees, causing the contract to pay out more than it collected.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker buys tickets with a referral scheme when `referralFee` is high (e.g., 10%). 2) Owner lowers `referralFee` to 0 (or attacker waits for a governance change). 3) Emergency mode is enabled. 4) Attacker calls `emergencyRefundTickets` and receives `ticketPrice * (1 - 0)` = full ticket price, even though referrers already received 10% at purchase. 5) Contract pays out more than it collected for those tickets.
hypotheses.impact: Contract insolvency during emergency refunds; referrers keep fees while users get full refunds, draining the pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: Store the referral fee (or the net amount paid) per ticket at purchase time, or snapshot `referralFee` per drawing in `DrawingState` and use that snapshot for refunds.

hypotheses.title: ticketOwner not cleared on burn or NFT owner mismatch in claimTickets
hypotheses.description: `_updateTicketOwnership` deletes `ticketOwner[ticketId]` and immediately `safeTransferFrom`s the NFT to `_recipient`. If `_recipient` is a contract whose `onERC721Received` reverts, the whole tx reverts — fine. But the bridge manager's `buyTickets` obtains ticket IDs from `jackpot.buyTickets(...)` and stores them in `userTickets[_recipient][currentDrawingId].ticketIds[...]`. Nothing updates `userTickets` on claim, so `getUserTickets` iterates stale entries. Worse, if a user has two claims and the second calls `claimTickets` again with the same IDs (already transferred), `_validateTicketOwnership` will pass only if `ticketOwner[id] == signer`; since the signer's entry was deleted, it fails — good. However, `safeTransferFrom` on the NFT will revert because the bridge manager no longer owns the NFT — the delete happens first, then transfer; state is inconsistent only within a failed call (reverted). The concrete bug is the unpruned `userTickets` list combined with `ticketOwner` deletion.
hypotheses.attackPath: User claims tickets; later calls `getUserTickets` which returns stale ticketIds; downstream they may submit the same IDs again to `claimWinnings`, which will call `_validateTicketOwnership` and revert on the not-owned one, wasting gas; more importantly, any external integrator reading `getUserTickets` may accidentally re-broadcast an already-claimed ticket.
hypotheses.impact: Off-chain integrations and batch claim builders get incorrect ownership data; users can be misled about which tickets they still own; possible gas waste and confusing revert paths.
hypotheses.recommendation: Maintain a compact/swap-and-pop `userTickets` list in `_updateTicketOwnership` so ownership lists remain authoritative; or require that `getUserTickets` filters by `ticketOwner` and returns a right-sized array.

hypotheses.title: claimWinnings does not verify signer is the caller or a fresh nonce
hypotheses.description: The function recovers `signer` from the signature and validates ticket ownership against `signer`, but never checks that `msg.sender == signer` or that the signer authorized this specific caller. Combined with the missing nonce, any relayer can execute a signed claim. While the funds go to the signed bridge destination, the user loses control over when and how the claim is executed, and the tickets are burned immediately.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User signs a claim but intends to execute it later. 2) Attacker front-runs and executes the claim with the same signature. 3) Tickets are burned and funds are bridged; the user cannot re-claim or change the bridge destination.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of user control over claim timing and destination; tickets burned prematurely.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `msg.sender == signer` or include `msg.sender` in the signed payload, and add a nonce/deadline.

hypotheses.title: Duplicate ticket prize pool top-up uses stale edgePerTicket
hypotheses.description: When a duplicate ticket is purchased, the code adds `_currentDrawingState.ticketPrice - _currentDrawingState.edgePerTicket` to the prize pool. `edgePerTicket` is set once in `_setNewDrawingState` as `lpEdgeTarget * ticketPrice / PRECISE_UNIT` using the ticket price at drawing initialization. If the owner changes `ticketPrice` mid-drawing via `setTicketPrice`, the new drawing state's `ticketPrice` is updated but `edgePerTicket` is not recalculated for the current drawing (only `_setNewDrawingState` sets it). Duplicate purchases then use the new `ticketPrice` with the old `edgePerTicket`, so the prize pool top-up is wrong — either over-crediting the prize pool (eroding LP edge) or under-crediting it (under-collateralizing winners).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Owner raises `ticketPrice` mid-drawing (a legitimate admin action). 2) Attacker buys a duplicate ticket. 3) The prize pool is credited `newTicketPrice - oldEdgePerTicket`, which is larger than `newTicketPrice * (1 - lpEdgeTarget)`. 4) The extra amount comes out of LP earnings, reducing LP edge. 5) Attacker can repeat to drain LP edge.
hypotheses.impact: LP edge erosion; prize pool over-crediting relative to LP earnings, potentially causing LP pool shortfall at settlement.
hypotheses.recommendation: Recompute `edgePerTicket` whenever `ticketPrice` changes for the current drawing, or store `edgePerTicket` per ticket at purchase time.

hypotheses.title: claimWinnings burns a ticket that pays zero in under-collateralized tiers
hypotheses.description: `claimWinnings` iterates over `_userTicketIds`, and for each ticket it burns the NFT and adds `winningAmount - referrerShare` to `totalClaimAmount`. `winningAmount` comes from `payoutCalculator.getTierPayout(drawingId, tierId)`, which is only set for tiers where `_tierWinners[i] != 0` at settlement. Any ticket whose tier had zero total winning tickets (possible for the bonusball-match variants of low `matches` when `minPayoutTiers[i]` is false and `premiumTierWeights[i]` is 0, or when no combination in that tier existed) will return a payout of 0, yet the ticket is still burned permanently with no reimbursement and no revert. The function never checks that `winningAmount > 0` before burning.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) An attacker monitors drawing mechanics and identifies a tier where `tierInfo.minPayoutTiers[i] == false` and `tierInfo.premiumTierWeights[i] == 0` (possible with owner-set weights that leave some low tiers at zero, since totalPayout loop sets payout only when `_tierWinners[i] != 0` and otherwise leaves `tierPayouts[_drawingId][i] == 0`). 2) The attacker purchases tickets that match only that tier (e.g., 0 normals + bonusball match) for the next drawing. 3) At settlement, `_tierWinners[i]` for that tier is non-zero only if at least one user ticket exists — but if the combination-count computation and `_dupResult` cancel such that the payout stored is 0 or negligible, the ticket is priced at zero. 4) The attacker (or any holder) calls `claimWinnings`, the NFT burns, no USDC is transferred, and the ticket is gone.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent loss of user tickets (burned) with zero payout; users who paid `ticketPrice` for the ticket receive nothing and cannot re-claim, effectively donating the ticket cost to LPs. Repeated across a batch, this drains ticket-holder value into the LP pool without consent.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `claimWinnings`, revert if `winningAmount == 0` (or do not burn the ticket when the tier payout is zero), so a user never pays gas and loses the NFT for nothing.

hypotheses.title: claimTickets signature is not bound to msg.sender allowing front-run griefing/hijack
hypotheses.description: `createClaimTicketEIP712Hash(_ticketIds, _recipient)` binds ticket IDs and recipient but not the caller. Anyone who observes the signature in the mempool can submit the exact same call before the legitimate user. Because the recipient is fixed by the signature, the attacker cannot steal the tickets for themselves, so the actual damage is limited to griefing: the honest user's transaction reverts (tickets already transferred) and they waste gas. The signed message contains no nonce or deadline, so signatures do not expire, but the state change (transfer + delete of `ticketOwner`) prevents reuse.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A ticket owner signs `(ticketIds, recipient)` intending to call `claimTickets`. 2) Attacker sees the pending tx, copies `_ticketIds`, `_recipient`, `_signature`, and front-runs with identical parameters. 3) Attacker's tx executes: NFTs go to intended recipient, `ticketOwner` cleaned. 4) Victim's tx reverts (or if owner already deleted, `NotTicketOwner`). Result: recipient still gets tickets, victim pays wasted gas.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing / wasted gas; no fund loss because recipient is bound to signature.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include `msg.sender` in the signed payload (or a nonce+deadline) so only the intended executor can consume the signature.

hypotheses.title: LP pool cap check ignores pending withdrawals, allowing over-cap deposits
hypotheses.description: `processDeposit` computes `totalPoolValue = lpPoolTotal + pendingDeposits` and rejects deposits exceeding `lpPoolCap`. It explicitly excludes `pendingWithdrawals` from this check (comment says "more conservative"), but pending withdrawals are still shares that will be converted to USDC at settlement and subtracted from `newLPValue`. Because the cap is meant to bound the LP pool's USDC exposure, ignoring pending withdrawals lets the effective pool exceed the cap: a user can deposit up to the cap while other LPs have large pending withdrawals, so the post-settlement LP value can exceed `lpPoolCap`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (LP) deposits up to `lpPoolCap`. 2) Attacker initiates a large withdrawal (pendingWithdrawal shares) — this does not reduce `lpPoolTotal` or `pendingDeposits`. 3) Attacker (or another LP) deposits again up to the cap, since the check only sees `lpPoolTotal + pendingDeposits`. 4) At settlement, pending withdrawals are converted and subtracted, but the new LP value can exceed the cap, and the cap invariant is broken.
hypotheses.impact: LP pool exceeds governance cap; risk exposure exceeds intended limits; `setLPPoolCap` may revert later when trying to lower the cap, and the protocol's risk model is violated.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include `pendingWithdrawals` (converted to USDC at the current accumulator) in the cap check, or track a separate "effective pool value" that accounts for pending withdrawals.

hypotheses.title: _bridgeFunds strict balance check blocks claims when bridge retains dust
hypotheses.description: _bridgeFunds() requires that the USDC balance decrease exactly equals _claimedAmount (preUSDCBalance - postUSDCBalance != _claimedAmount reverts). If the bridge provider's call transfers slightly less (e.g., due to fee-on-transfer USDC, rounding, or a bridge that takes a fee), the entire claimWinnings transaction reverts. Since the bridge details are supplied by the user and signed, a user whose bridge route has any fee or rounding will be permanently unable to claim winnings through this contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User signs a claim with bridgeDetails pointing to a bridge that deducts a small fee. 2) claimWinnings executes, jackpot.claimWinnings succeeds, but _bridgeFunds sees a balance delta less than claimedAmount. 3) Transaction reverts; the user's tickets remain unclaimed and the signed message is consumed only on success, so retries with the same signature also fail.
hypotheses.impact: Users with fee-charging bridge routes cannot claim winnings; funds remain stuck in the bridge manager until a different bridge route is used, and the strict equality check makes the contract brittle to any USDC behavior change.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow the balance delta to be >= claimedAmount minus a small tolerance, or transfer the exact claimedAmount to the bridge and let the bridge handle fees.

hypotheses.title: emergencyRefundTickets reverts on any non-current-drawing ticket in batch
hypotheses.description: emergencyRefundTickets() loops over user-supplied ticket IDs and reverts if any ticket's drawingId != currentDrawingId. A user who holds a mix of current-drawing and past-drawing tickets cannot refund the current-drawing ones in a single batch; the presence of one past-drawing ticket reverts the entire call. Since emergency mode is the recovery path, this can trap users who cannot easily enumerate which of their tickets are from the current drawing.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) During emergency mode, user submits a batch containing one ticket from a prior drawing (e.g., a losing ticket they forgot about). 2) The loop reverts on TicketNotEligibleForRefund. 3) User must manually filter tickets; if they cannot (e.g., via a contract that batches all their tickets), their current-drawing funds remain stuck.
hypotheses.impact: Users with mixed-drawing ticket batches cannot refund current-drawing tickets in one transaction, delaying or blocking recovery of their funds during emergency mode.
hypotheses.recommendation: Skip ineligible tickets instead of reverting, or emit an event and continue the loop.

hypotheses.title: EIP-712 domain lacks chainId/verifyingContract binding for cross-chain replay
hypotheses.description: The EIP-712 domain is constructed with only `_name` and `_version`; OpenZeppelin's EIP712 includes `chainId` and `verifyingContract` by default, so this is actually mitigated. However, the contract is explicitly designed for cross-chain use ("Cross-chain jackpot bridge"), and the signed payloads do not include a chain identifier or the destination chain. If the same `JackpotBridgeManager` is deployed on multiple chains with the same name/version and the same address (e.g., via CREATE2), a signature valid on one chain is valid on another, allowing cross-chain replay of `claimWinnings` and `claimTickets`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User signs a claim on Chain A. 2) Attacker replays the same signature on Chain B where the same contract is deployed at the same address with the same domain. 3) If the user has tickets on Chain B (or the ticketId collides), the claim executes on Chain B without the user's intent.
hypotheses.impact: Cross-chain replay of claims and ticket transfers; unauthorized fund movement on the destination chain.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include the destination chainId in the signed struct, or ensure the EIP-712 domain differs per chain (e.g., include chainId in the name/version).

hypotheses.title: Protocol fee transferred before LP settlement can cause underflow
hypotheses.description: `_transferProtocolFee` transfers `protocolFeeAmount` to `protocolFeeAddress` *before* `jackpotLPManager.processDrawingSettlement` is called. The settlement computes `postDrawLpValue = lpPoolTotal + lpEarnings - userWinnings - protocolFeeAmount`. If `userWinnings + protocolFeeAmount > lpPoolTotal + lpEarnings`, this underflows and reverts, but the protocol fee has already been transferred out. More subtly, if `lpEarnings` is small and `userWinnings` is large (e.g., a jackpot hit), the protocol fee is taken from LP pool value, potentially leaving the pool insolvent for pending withdrawals. The fee is computed on `lpEarnings - userWinnings - protocolFeeThreshold`, which can be positive even when the overall pool is in deficit, because `lpEarnings` only reflects ticket revenue for the current drawing, not the full pool.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker buys tickets to inflate `lpEarnings` in a drawing. 2) A large win occurs (`userWinnings` > `lpEarnings`). 3) `_transferProtocolFee` sees `lpEarnings > userWinnings` is false, so no fee — but if `lpEarnings` is just above `userWinnings + threshold`, a fee is taken from the pool. 4) The pool's `lpPoolTotal` is reduced by the fee, and pending withdrawals may not be fully backed. 5) LPs cannot withdraw their full shares.
hypotheses.impact: LP pool insolvency; pending withdrawals under-collateralized; protocol fee taken from LP principal rather than profit.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the protocol fee based on the *net* pool value after accounting for all liabilities (pending withdrawals, user winnings), or transfer the fee only after settlement confirms the pool remains solvent.

hypotheses.title: claimWinnings balance-diff check is bypassable via reentrant-like token or self-transfer
hypotheses.description: The function verifies `preUSDCBalance - postUSDCBalance == _claimedAmount` on the *same contract* balance. The call target (`_bridgeDetails.to`) is fully attacker-controlled because `_bridgeDetails` is signed by the ticket owner but constructed by the caller. A malicious ticket owner can sign a transaction whose `to` is `usdc` itself (i.e. call `transfer(address(this), amount)` — USDC allows self-transfer), causing the bridge manager's balance to remain unchanged only if returned. Here the balance actually decreases then increases within the call if `to` is a contract that re-transfers; but more simply, if the bridge target returns the USDC to the bridge manager inside the same call (any contract the owner controls), `preUSDCBalance - postUSDCBalance` equals `_claimedAmount` (since it left) and then the owner can still retrieve it in a separate call... Actually the check compares pre and post *after* the call, so the returned USDC would be back and the check fails. However, the owner can set `to = usdc` and `data = transferFrom(address(this), attacker, claimed)` only if allowance exists to attacker; instead the owner sets `approveTo = attacker` (signed) then calls USDA's `transferFrom(address(this), attacker, amount)` via `to = usdc` — but the bridge manager's msg.sender for user-controlled `to=usdc` is the bridge manager itself, so `transferFrom(bridgeManager, attacker)` requires allowance that bridgeManager gave to... itself cannot grant. The real gap: `approveTo` is never reset, so a previously approved `approveTo` retains allowance.
hypotheses.attackPath: A ticket owner signs a claim with `approveTo = E`, `to = E`, `data = E.useAllowance()`. First call E pulls max USDC using the residual allowance from a prior claim. The check `pre - post != claimedAmount` can still pass because the amount transferred out happens to be `claimedAmount` (bridge target drains exactly claimedAmount). Since the amount drained equals `claimedAmount`, the check passes. Because the check only verifies *magnitude of outflow* rather than *destination*, the ERC-20 has already gone to an attacker-controlled address while the accounting believes a legit bridge occurred.
hypotheses.impact: Divergence between intent (bridge to destination chain) and outcome (USDC sent to arbitrary signer-chosen address). Combined with a signed `RelayTxData.to` the signer can route funds anywhere the `to` contract allows; the check provides no protection that funds reached a real bridge.
hypotheses.recommendation: Do not rely solely on magnitude of balance delta; whitelist bridge destinations/selectors or verify a bridge-emitted event, and always reset prior approvals to zero after the bridge call.

hypotheses.title: getLPValueBreakdown uses wrong accumulator for pending withdrawals
hypotheses.description: For `pendingWithdrawals`, the function values same-round pending withdrawal shares using `drawingAccumulator[currentDrawingId - 1]`. However, `processDrawingSettlement` converts pending withdrawals using the *new* accumulator computed for the settled drawing (`newAccumulator`), which is `drawingAccumulator[_drawingId - 1] * postDrawLpValue / lpPoolTotal`. These differ whenever the drawing's LP value changes. The view therefore under- or over-reports the LP's pending withdrawal value, misleading LPs and integrators.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable for profit, but an LP relying on this view to decide whether to initiate additional withdrawals may make incorrect decisions; integrators displaying LP value will show wrong numbers.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect accounting display; potential for LPs to mis-time withdrawals; no direct fund loss but breaks the "view reflects reality" invariant.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the projected new accumulator the same way `processDrawingSettlement` does (using current `lpPoolTotal`, `lpEarnings`, `userWinnings`, `protocolFeeAmount` if available) or document that the value is a lower/upper bound.

hypotheses.title: buyTickets accepts user-selected ticket price via stale drawing state, enabling underpayment
hypotheses.category: Price used before it is updated / stale pricing
hypotheses.description: `buyTickets` reads `currentDrawingState.ticketPrice` to compute `ticketsValue = numTicketsBought * currentDrawingState.ticketPrice` and transfers that USDC from the caller. Meanwhile the global `ticketPrice` is what actually governs the next drawing’s economics (`_setNewDrawingState` copies the global `ticketPrice` into the new drawing state). If the owner raises the global `ticketPrice` mid-drawing (a routine governance action, allowed by `setTicketPrice` at any time and only blocked when `jackpotLock` is set), the currently active drawing’s `ticketPrice` snapshots the old value. Any user who calls `buyTickets` between `setTicketPrice` and the next `_setNewDrawingState` pays the OLD price, and the drawing’s `lpEarnings`/`prizePool` accounting credits the old amount, while the protocol’s intended new price is not honored. There is no per-drawing re-snapshot on purchase.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker monitors the mempool / off-chain for a `setTicketPrice` transaction (or simply observes the change and the next drawing’s parameters). 2) Attacker front-runs the settlement (`scaledEntropyCallback` → `_setNewDrawingState`) and calls `buyTickets` in bulk while `drawingState[currentDrawingId].ticketPrice` is still the old lower value. 3) Attacker receives the same number of tickets for less USDC than the newly configured price. 4) Because `lpEarnings` and `prizePool` are credited at the old, lower price, the protocol is short the intended revenue.
hypotheses.impact: Direct revenue shortfall for the current drawing; new price is not enforced for tickets purchased during the window, allowing mass underpayment when the owner intends a price increase.
hypotheses.recommendation: When `setTicketPrice` is called for the active drawing, either re-snapshot `drawingState[currentDrawingId].ticketPrice` (and dependent values) or disallow price changes for the current drawing (e.g., only apply to next drawing via a pending value).

hypotheses.title: No sequencer/staleness check on entropy callback means settlement can be blocked or delayed
hypotheses.description: `scaledEntropyCallback` is the sole settlement path and requires `currentDrawingState.jackpotLock == true` plus `msg.sender == address(entropy)`. If the Pyth entropy callback is never delivered (provider downtime, L2 sequencer outage, gas limit too low so `CallbackFailed` reverts on the provider side leaving the request pending forever), the drawing stays locked permanently. There is no fallback path, no timeout, no admin/participant-triggered re-request, and no sequencer uptime check anywhere in the code. The `runJackpot` function can be called only once per drawing (lock prevents re-request), so a single failed callback bricks the drawing.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) An attacker observes that `entropyBaseGasLimit + entropyVariableGasLimit * bonusballMax` is close to the actual callback cost. 2) Attacker grinds MEV / manipulates `bonusballMax` via influence over LP deposits (raising `bonusballMax` via large deposits in a buyer’s own draw) so that the callback’s real cost exceeds the configured gas limit, causing the provider’s callback to revert. 3) Once the callback reverts and the sequence is consumed, `runJackpot` cannot be re-invoked for the same drawing (the lock check reverts), and entropy is not re-requested. 4) Tickets for that drawing remain locked; refunds require `enableEmergencyMode()` (owner-only), so an untrusted actor’s goal is denial-of-service / forced emergency shutdown.
hypotheses.impact: Drawing is frozen; all tickets in the current drawing are unclaimable, LP deposits/withdrawals are frozen, and the only recovery is owner-driven emergency mode which itself blocks all normal operations. Users’ funds and ticket NFTs are effectively locked.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a permissionless re-request path (e.g., allow `runJackpot` to be called again if the current drawing is locked and a timeout has elapsed, or add a dedicated `reRequestEntropy` that calls `entropy.requestAndCallbackScaledRandomness` again) and/or track a request sequence so a failed callback can be retried without owner intervention.

hypotheses.title: _bridgeFunds trusts post-call balance delta without enforcing exact recipient
hypotheses.description: `_bridgeFunds` checks that `preUSDCBalance - postUSDCBalance == _claimedAmount` but places no constraint on who actually received the USDC, nor on the calldata being a legitimate bridge interaction. The `_bridgeDetails.to` and `_bridgeDetails.data` are fully user-supplied and only the signature of the ticket owner is required — and the ticket owner can be the same actor as the caller. If `_bridgeDetails.approveTo != address(0)`, the contract approves `approveTo` for `_claimedAmount` immediately before the call, so any contract referenced in `approveTo` can `transferFrom` the manager during `_bridgeDetails.to.call(...)`, draining the winnings to an attacker-controlled address while satisfying the balance-delta check (the USDC simply leaves the manager). There is no allowlist of bridge providers, no check that `approveTo` and `to` agree, and no minimum-received / slippage parameter.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) An attacker with a claimable winning ticket signs an EIP-712 payload where `bridgeDetails.approveTo` is an attacker contract, `bridgeDetails.to` is the same or a cooperating contract, and `data` calls `usdc.transferFrom(address(this), attacker, claimedAmount)` (via the approval just granted). 2) Attacker calls `claimWinnings`. 3) `jackpot.claimWinnings` pays USDC to `JackpotBridgeManager`, `_bridgeFunds` approves the attacker contract, then the attacker’s call executes the transferFrom and moves funds to the attacker. 4) The balance delta check passes because USDC left the manager by exactly `claimedAmount`. 5) The `FundsBridged` event misleadingly reports `_bridgeDetails.to` as the recipient, and no cross-chain transfer occurred.
hypotheses.impact: Winnings are routed to an arbitrary address rather than a real bridge; if a user is tricked into signing a malicious payload (e.g., via a phishing dApp that constructs `bridgeDetails` for them), their winnings are stolen. Worse, any relayer who cosigns or submits such a payload on the user’s behalf will route the winnings to the attacker without any slippage/min-out protection.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce an owner-managed allowlist of `(approveTo, to)` bridge pairs (or at least require `approveTo == to` or `approveTo == address(0)`), and validate the calldata against a known bridge selector/route before approving and calling. Optionally require the destination recipient encoded in `data` to equal `_bridgeDetails.to` and enforce a minimum received amount.

hypotheses.title: claimWinnings reads USDC balance delta but jackpot.claimWinnings can be re-entered via NFT burn callback
hypotheses.description: `claimWinnings` computes `claimedAmount` as the USDC balance delta around `jackpot.claimWinnings(_userTicketIds)`. Inside `Jackpot.claimWinnings`, `jackpotNFT.burnTicket(ticketId)` is called, which triggers `_beforeTokenTransfer`/`_afterTokenTransfer` on the NFT. If the NFT contract (or a future upgrade) invokes a callback, or if `payoutCalculator.getTierPayout` is a malicious/upgradeable contract, the attacker can re-enter `JackpotBridgeManager.claimWinnings` (guarded) — but more importantly, the balance-delta accounting is fragile: any USDC sent to the bridge manager during the call (e.g., via a re-entrant `claimReferralFees` on Jackpot that transfers to the bridge manager) inflates `claimedAmount`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker arranges for `referralFees[bridgeManager]` to be non-zero (e.g., by setting the bridge manager as a referrer on a ticket purchase). 2) Attacker calls `claimWinnings`; during `jackpot.claimWinnings`, the attacker re-enters `Jackpot.claimReferralFees()` (not guarded against the bridge manager being a referrer) which transfers USDC to the bridge manager. 3) `postUSDCBalance - preUSDCBalance` now includes the referral fee, inflating `claimedAmount`. 4) `_bridgeFunds` bridges the inflated amount, and the balance check passes because the extra USDC was legitimately received.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker bridges more USDC than their actual winnings, draining referral fees or other USDC held by the bridge manager.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track claimed amounts via return values from `jackpot.claimWinnings` rather than balance deltas, or snapshot and exclude non-claim USDC inflows.

hypotheses.title: claimWinnings reverts on zero-payout tickets, bricking batch claims
hypotheses.description: claimWinnings() iterates over user-supplied ticket IDs and calls jackpotNFT.burnTicket(ticketId) for each before transferring the total. If any ticket in the batch has a zero tier payout (e.g., a losing ticket), the loop still burns it and adds 0 to totalClaimAmount, but the final usdc.safeTransfer(msg.sender, totalClaimAmount) will revert if totalClaimAmount is 0. More importantly, a user who batches a winning ticket with a losing ticket will have the losing ticket burned and the winning ticket burned, but the transfer reverts, so the entire batch is rolled back — however, if the user batches only losing tickets, the burn succeeds and the transfer reverts, wasting gas but not funds. The real griefing vector is that a user cannot selectively claim without knowing tier payouts, and any revert in the loop (e.g., from a ticket already burned by a prior partial claim) blocks the whole batch.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or any user) submits a batch containing a ticket that has already been burned (e.g., via a prior claim) or a ticket whose ownerOf check fails. 2) The loop reverts on ownerOf or burnTicket, blocking the entire batch. 3) Users with mixed valid/invalid tickets cannot claim their valid winnings in one tx.
hypotheses.impact: Users are forced to claim tickets one-by-one; a single bad ticket in a batch blocks all claims in that batch, and repeated griefing can make batch claiming unusable.
hypotheses.recommendation: Skip tickets with zero payout or already-burned status instead of reverting, or require callers to pre-filter tickets.

hypotheses.title: Emergency LP withdrawal can underflow lpPoolTotal for drawing 0
hypotheses.description: In `emergencyWithdrawLP`, for `_drawingId == 0`, the code subtracts `lp.lastDeposit.amount` from `lpDrawingState[0].pendingDeposits`. However, if the LP's `lastDeposit` was already consolidated into `consolidatedShares` (e.g., via a prior `processDeposit` in a later drawing, or if `_consolidateDeposits` was called), `pendingDeposits` for drawing 0 may not contain that amount, causing an underflow revert. More critically, for `_drawingId > 0`, the code subtracts `sharesToUsdc` from `lpDrawingState[_drawingId].lpPoolTotal` and `withdrawalToUsdc` from `lpPoolTotal`, but if multiple LPs emergency-withdraw, the `lpPoolTotal` can be driven to zero or underflow because the accumulator-based conversion may not match the actual pool total (especially if the pool had losses). This can revert, freezing LP funds during emergency.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Emergency mode is enabled. 2) Multiple LPs call `emergencyWithdrawLP`. 3) The first few withdrawals succeed, but as `lpPoolTotal` is decremented, a later withdrawal's `sharesToUsdc` exceeds the remaining `lpPoolTotal`, causing an underflow revert. 4) Remaining LPs cannot withdraw their funds.
hypotheses.impact: Frozen LP funds during emergency; LPs unable to recover deposits.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap the withdrawal amount at the remaining `lpPoolTotal`, or use a pro-rata distribution mechanism that cannot underflow.

hypotheses.title: jackpotLock bypass by calling lockJackpot then unlockJackpot leaves pending randomness request
hypotheses.description: `runJackpot()` locks, then requests randomness from the entropy provider. The provider will eventually call `scaledEntropyCallback` which requires `jackpotLock == true`. The owner can call `unlockJackpot()` after `runJackpot()` to unlock, letting users buy/deposit for a drawing that already requested randomness. When the entropy callback arrives, it will use the current (post-buy) `drawingState[currentDrawingId]` and `drawingEntries[currentDrawingId]` — including tickets bought after the entropy request — to compute winnings. This allows tickets to be purchased *after* the randomness request, without the owner's consent even needed if the owner is tricked into unlocking, but more precisely: any actor who calls the owner cannot do this directly. However, the owner-only path is the only path, so it requires owner action; per rules, owner is trusted. Still, an untrusted actor can call `runJackpot` and observe the lock, then any subsequent unlock by the owner allows untrusted purchase during the pending window, corrupting fairness. This is a genuine state inconsistency between "locked" and "randomness in-flight".
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker calls `runJackpot` when due, then waits for the owner to unlock (e.g., legitimate maintenance). During the unlocked window, attacker purchases tickets for the current drawing at known cheap prices; because the randomness is already committed but not yet delivered, the attacker increases their share of winning tickets (especially duplicates) before the callback computes userWinnings, diluting winnings calculations against the new ticket set.
hypotheses.impact: Manipulation of the drawing outcome distribution; possible large swings in tier payouts and LP accounting; wrong tier payouts recorded. Though owner-triggered in part, the untrusted attacker is the beneficiary and can time purchases to known pending entropy.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a separate `entropyRequested` flag set in `runJackpot` and checked in `unlockJackpot`, or disallow unlocks while the request is in flight.

hypotheses.title: Jackpot.claimWinnings lacks per-ticket dedup when tierPayout is zero — can be used to burn NFTs nobody wants
hypotheses.description: Any NFT owner of an old-drawing ticket can call `claimWinnings` even when `tierPayout == 0`, permanently burning the NFT for zero payout. This is not a privilege escalation — the owner is authorized — but it does allow a griefing context if ticket ownership was just transferred (e.g., via `claimTickets` race in the bridge manager) where an intermediate holder burns before the recipient can claim. Since only the current owner can call, this requires the attacker to actually own the ticket.
hypotheses.attackPath: Requires ownership; not exploitable by unprivileged third party against a victim's ticket.
hypotheses.impact: Minimal; owner-only self-harm.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert if computed payout is zero to prevent accidental burns.

hypotheses.title: Bridge manager's _bridgeFunds balance check can be bypassed by rebasing/fee-on-transfer USDC
hypotheses.description: `_bridgeFunds` verifies that `preUSDCBalance - postUSDCBalance == _claimedAmount`. This assumes USDC is a strict, non-rebasing, non-fee-on-transfer token. If the configured `usdc` token ever rebases, charges transfer fees, or if the bridge call itself moves additional USDC out of the contract (e.g., a malicious `_bridgeDetails.to` that calls `transferFrom` on the manager via a pre-existing approval), the equality check fails and the entire claim reverts — or, if the bridge call moves *less* than `_claimedAmount` but the difference is masked by an incoming transfer, the check passes while funds are not fully bridged.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker crafts `_bridgeDetails.to` as a contract that, during the call, transfers a small amount of USDC *into* the manager (e.g., from a pre-funded helper) while only bridging part of `_claimedAmount`. 2) `preUSDCBalance - postUSDCBalance` equals `_claimedAmount` because the incoming transfer offsets the shortfall. 3) Attacker's signature authorizes the bridge details, so the manager executes it; the attacker keeps the unbridged USDC in the manager (or extracts it later via another claim).
hypotheses.impact: Partial bridging with full accounting credit; USDC stuck in the manager or extractable by the attacker; winnings not actually delivered to the destination chain.
hypotheses.recommendation: Instead of relying on balance deltas, transfer `_claimedAmount` to the bridge target explicitly and verify the target received it, or use a pull-based bridge pattern where the manager only approves and the bridge pulls exactly `_claimedAmount`.

hypotheses.title: Jackpot.claimWinnings burns NFT before computing payout, allowing reentrancy via NFT hooks
hypotheses.description: In `Jackpot.claimWinnings`, the loop calls `jackpotNFT.burnTicket(ticketId)` before `payoutCalculator.getTierPayout` and before accumulating `totalClaimAmount`. `burnTicket` triggers ERC-721 `_beforeTokenTransfer`/`_afterTokenTransfer` hooks. If the NFT contract or a hook recipient is malicious (or if `jackpotNFT` is ever upgraded), the attacker can re-enter `claimWinnings` for other tickets or re-enter `emergencyRefundTickets` (if emergency mode is on) before `totalClaimAmount` is finalized. The `nonReentrant` guard on `claimWinnings` blocks direct re-entry, but `emergencyRefundTickets` is a separate `nonReentrant` function — cross-function reentrancy is possible if the attacker can toggle emergency mode (they cannot) or if another unguarded function exists.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker owns tickets in a completed drawing. 2) Attacker calls `claimWinnings`; during `burnTicket`, the NFT hook re-enters `Jackpot.claimReferralFees()` (unguarded against reentrancy from the NFT contract) which transfers USDC out. 3) The outer `claimWinnings` then transfers `totalClaimAmount` computed from stale state. 4) Alternatively, if `payoutCalculator` is malicious/upgradeable, it can re-enter and manipulate `tierPayouts` before the outer call reads them.
hypotheses.impact: Double-spend of winnings or referral fees, potentially draining the jackpot's USDC balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute all payouts and accumulate `totalClaimAmount` before burning NFTs, and ensure `jackpotNFT` and `payoutCalculator` are trusted/immutable.

hypotheses.title: runJackpot refunds excess ETH via arbitrary call before entropy request
hypotheses.description: `runJackpot` is `nonReentrant`, but it performs `payable(msg.sender).call{value: msg.value - fee}("")` to refund excess ETH BEFORE calling `entropy.requestAndCallbackScaledRandomness`. The refund call is an external call to an attacker-controlled address. Although `nonReentrant` blocks re-entry into `runJackpot`, the attacker can re-enter other unguarded functions such as `claimReferralFees` (which is `nonReentrant` — blocked) or `initiateWithdraw` (not `nonReentrant`). More importantly, the refund happens after `_lockJackpot()` but before the entropy request, so if the refund call reverts or consumes gas, the drawing is locked but no entropy request is made, leaving the jackpot stuck.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `runJackpot` with `msg.value > fee` from a contract whose `receive()` reverts or consumes all gas. 2) The refund call fails, reverting the whole transaction — but `_lockJackpot()` already set `jackpotLock = true` in the same transaction, so the revert undoes it. 3) Alternatively, the attacker's `receive()` re-enters `initiateWithdraw` (not `nonReentrant`) to manipulate LP state while the drawing is locked. 4) The attacker can also front-run the entropy request by observing the mempool and calling `initiateWithdraw` in the same block.
hypotheses.impact: LP state manipulation during drawing lock, or griefing by forcing reverts that leave the jackpot in an inconsistent state.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move the ETH refund to the end of the function (after the entropy request) or use a pull-based refund pattern.

hypotheses.title: Referral scheme ID collision due to unsorted referrer arrays allows reuse of stored scheme
hypotheses.description: The referral scheme hash is `keccak256(abi.encode(_referrers, _referralSplit))`, computed over the caller-provided ordering. Two callers can supply the same set of referrers in different orders (or with a trivial zero-split rejection prevented, but reordering is not), producing different hashes but identical economic meaning. Conversely, the same hash can be produced by different (referrers, splits) pairs only via collision, which is infeasible. The real issue: since `referralSchemes[referralSchemeId]` is only populated when `referrers.length == 0`, and it is keyed by this user-chosen hash, an attacker can craft permutations to inflate the mapping with schemes they control, but more importantly in `_payReferrersWinnings`, when the scheme is looked up by the ticket's stored `_referralSchemeId`, no check exists that the scheme existing at the moment of payout matches what was intended — but the hash was fixed at mint, so that's safe. Instead, note that `referralSplit` sum must equal PRECISE_UNIT which is enforced at purchase; fine.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker supplies a referral scheme where they are the referrer and the ticket owner; the win-share is paid to the attacker. Not exploitable in principle because the signer chose the scheme. But a stale scheme cannot be resurrected since the hash pins the exact arrays. The concrete risk is in JackpotBridgeManager: `claimWinnings` passes user-supplied ticket IDs and the payout path in Jackpot reads referral scheme from the minted ticket, not from the claim input, so no injection.
hypotheses.impact: No direct exploit observed; scheme hash binds arrays exactly. Lower priority.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only relevant if new logic relies on scheme identity; document ordering requirement.

hypotheses.title: JackpotBridgeManager.buyTickets approves Jackpot for exact ticketCost but stale allowance could persist
hypotheses.description: `usdc.approve(address(jackpot), ticketCost)` is executed before `jackpot.buyTickets`. The Jackpot pulls exactly `ticketCost`. If the Jackpot implementation ever pulled less than `ticketCost` (e.g., due to a future upgrade of the immutable Jackpot), residual allowance would remain and could be exploited by a future jackpot upgrade or by any other call path that the bridge manager makes. Since `jackpot` here is immutable, the risk is bounded, but the allowance is left nonzero (not reset to zero after) which is a standing approval. No untrusted actor can currently drain it since Jackpot is fixed and pulls exact amount — but this is a latent risk.
hypotheses.attackPath: No current exploit against the fixed Jackpot; requires Jackpot to under-pull, which it does not.
hypotheses.impact: Latent; no immediate loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Set allowance to zero after the call: `usdc.approve(address(jackpot), 0)`.

hypotheses.title: JackpotLPManager.initializeLP is callable by Jackpot only and Jackpot.initializeLPDeposits is owner-gated; no untrusted path
hypotheses.description: `initializeLP()` (external onlyJackpot) sets `drawingAccumulator[0] = PRECISE_UNIT` with no idempotency guard. If the Jackpot owner ever calls `initializeLPDeposits` twice it would revert at the accumulator check, so the duplicate-init path is blocked at the Jackpot level. Untrusted callers cannot reach `initializeLP` because of `onlyJackpot`. Therefore there is no untrusted-caller re-init vector here.
hypotheses.attackPath: N/A — only Jackpot can call, and Jackpot guards single initialization.
hypotheses.impact: None from untrusted actors.
hypotheses.recommendation: Optional defense-in-depth: add `if (drawingAccumulator[0] != 0) revert` inside `initializeLP`.

hypotheses.title: ScaledEntropyProvider stores callback as msg.sender at request time; Jackpot's runJackpot is permissionless so any third party can force a draw
hypotheses.description: `runJackpot()` is documented as permissionless and any address can invoke it once the drawing time has passed. This is by design (keeperless execution), but the caller must pay the Pyth entropy fee and receives an ETH refund of excess. The important boundary check is that `scaledEntropyCallback` has `onlyEntropy` so randomness cannot be spoofed. However, the callback's `nonReentrant` + `jackpotLock` guard means double-execution is prevented. There is no untrusted-actor capability gain beyond triggering on time.
hypotheses.attackPath: Honest permissionless liveness; no privilege escalation, no fund theft.
hypotheses.impact: None beyond gas griefing (attacker pays their own fee).
hypotheses.recommendation: Document intent; optionally restrict to a keeper role, but not security-critical.
